item.title: Applicative theories can count
item.description: arXiv:2611.10711v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Applicative theories offer a proof-theoretic framework for studying complexity. In this paper, we introduce a family of applicative theories to characterize classes ranging from constant-depth circuits to polynomial space. Our approach relies on a simple axiom scheme, the small variations of which allows to capture various forms of counting and alternation. This leads to highly uniform results. When applied on notation, the scheme captures bit counting, yielding a characterization of the functions computable by constant-depth, polynomial-size threshold circuits ($\textbf{FTC}^0$); when applied lexicographically, it allows for the counting of accepting computations, yielding a characterization of the functions in the counting hierarchy ($\textbf{FCH}$). Increasing the logical complexity of the induction formulas allowed in the scheme, we obtain characterizations of the functions computable by bounded Boolean circuits of logarithmic-depth and polynomial-size ($\textbf{FNC}^1$) and of the functions computable in polynomial space ($\textbf{FPSPACE}$). The latter characterization solves an open problem in the field. Finally, we investigate separation results. While it is unknown whether $\textbf{FNC}^1$ and $\textbf{FCH}$ are different, there is an oracle relative to which (relativized) $\textbf{FNC}^1$ is strictly contained in (relativized) $\textbf{FCH}$. We use this fact to separate the theories characterizing them, by exploring their ability to represent higher-order functionals.
item.dc:creator: Melissa Antonelli, Marcel Ertel, Eduardo Skapinakis

item.title: Decidability of Elementary Modal Logics is Undecidable
item.description: arXiv:2611.11199v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the decidability of modal satisfiability over classes of Kripke frames defined by universal first-order sentences. Although some such classes yield undecidable satisfiability problems, decidability is guaranteed for wide families of frame conditions, including universal Horn sentences and universal sentences implying transitivity. A more than decade-old open problem asks a natural question: can decidable and undecidable cases be distinguished algorithmically? We prove that this is impossible, already for equality-free universal frame conditions over a single binary relation. More precisely, there is no algorithm that, given such a condition, decides whether its associated local modal satisfiability problem is decidable. We first establish the result for conditions with equality and then eliminate equality by passing to quotients of worlds with identical incoming and outgoing edges.
item.dc:creator: Jakub Michaliszyn

item.title: Addressing Bias Early in the AI Lifecycle: Social Determinants of Health in Functional and Cognitive Assessment Labels of Nursing Home Residents
item.description: arXiv:2611.11535v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fairness in clinical artificial intelligence (AI) is usually evaluated after model training, yet bias can enter earlier in the AI lifecycle, during data collection and labelling. When routine clinical assessments serve as target variables, systematic differences in these labels across sociodemographic groups are carried into model development, validation and updating. This study addresses this early lifecycle stage by auditing labels from three standardised instruments used in residential care: the Barthel Index (BI), the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and the Global Deterioration Scale (GDS). Using electronic health records of 2,407 residents from 12 nursing homes in the Basque Country, Spain (2011-2021), we assessed four social determinants of health (SDoH) - sex, educational attainment, lifetime work activity and marital status - with two group fairness metrics, Disparate Impact (DI) and Statistical Parity Difference (SPD), computed for each outcome category with bootstrap confidence intervals. Disparities were found for all four attributes and across the three instruments: men, residents with intermediate education and never-partnered residents were more frequently classified in categories indicating preserved function or cognition. These disparities may reflect genuine differences in health status, measurement properties of the instruments, assessment practices or selective admission to residential care, and cannot be attributed to a single cause with the present design. Regardless of their origin, any model trained on these labels would inherit them, and they could persist through later lifecycle stages unless explicitly examined. These findings support pre-training label auditing as the first step of a continuous fairness assessment spanning model development, validation, deployment and updating.
item.dc:creator: Isabel Amaya-Rodr\'iguez, Cristina Martin, Nekane Larburu, Teresa Garcia-Navarro, Roberto Gonz\'alez Novas, Alberto Rodr\'iguez Taboada, Maite Garc\'ia-Sebastian, Ainara Estanga, Mirian Ecay-Torres, Pablo Mart\'inez-Lage, Miguel A. Armengol de la Hoz, Cristina Rubio-Escudero, Iv\'an Mac\'ia

item.title: Spectral Stability, Fatou Basin Contraction, and Machine-Checked Multipliers in Holomorphic Extensions of Generalized Syracuse Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.11641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We embed the Syracuse operator $T(n) = n/2$ (even $n$), $T(n) = (3n+1)/2$ (odd $n$) and the Collatz map $C(n)$ into $\mathbb{C}$ via entire functions of exponential type $\pi$: $f(z) = \frac{1}{4}(1 + 4z - (1 + 2z)\cos(\pi z))$ and $F(z) = \frac{1}{4}(2 + 7z - (2 + 5z)\cos(\pi z))$. We prove five results: (1) every integer periodic cycle $C \subset \mathbb{N}^+$ of $T$ is a strictly attracting Fatou cycle of $f$ with multiplier $\mu_f(C) = 3^{N_{\mathrm{odd}}}/2^N = \prod_{n \in C\text{ odd}} \frac{3n}{3n+1} \in (0,1)$, and $\mu_f(O_{1,2}) = \mu_F(O_{1,4,2}) = 3/4 < 1$; (2) on the Fatou basin $B(O_{1,2})$, $g = f^{\circ 2}$ conjugates to $\Phi_j(g(z)) = \frac{3}{4}\Phi_j(z)$ with Koenigs Taylor jets $c_2(1) = -\frac{13}{2}\pi^2$ and $d_2(2) = -\frac{9}{2}\pi^2$; (3) the Schwarzian derivative is strictly negative on $\mathbb{Z}$ ($S(f)(n) \le 3\pi^2 - \frac{3}{8}\pi^4 \approx -6.9196 < 0$), and a repelling Julia 2-cycle $O_{\mathrm{rep}} \subset J(f)$ ($\mu \approx 1.2148 > 1$) isolates $B(O_{1,2})$; (4) on $(\mathbb{Z}_2, \mu_{\mathrm{Haar}})$, the 2-adic Lyapunov exponent $\lambda_{\mathrm{Haar}} = \frac{1}{2}\ln(3/4) \approx -0.143841 < 0$ equals $\frac{1}{2}\ln|\mu_f(O_{1,2})|$; and (5) we certify 20 theorems in Lean 4 (anc/CollatzAttractor.lean, 0 sorry). These results establish local Fatou invariants and 2-adic ergodic averages for $f(z)$, leaving open whether every $n_0 \in \mathbb{N}^+$ lies in $\bigcup_{k \ge 0} f^{-k}(B(O_{1,2}))$.
item.dc:creator: Volkan Da\u{g}l{\i}, Zerrin Da\u{g}l{\i}, Da\u{g}han Da\u{g}l{\i}, Emrah Yurtseven, Murat Emre \"Ozkaya

item.title: Declarative DNS - Resolving Recursive Resolution
item.description: arXiv:2611.11689v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: DNS zone configuration errors are a frequent source of outages and frustration, particularly in combination with DNSSEC. Research has attempted to address the problem of zone configuration errors using formal methods, but existing proposals (i) only verify the absence of specific, known configuration errors, and (ii) do not consider DNSSEC. We present a new formal model of the DNS that covers most of DNSSEC, making it one of the most complete DNS models to date. In addition, we present a new tool, DecDNS, that performs a resolvability change-impact analysis of zone configuration updates using our model. We show that such a change-impact analysis can identify configuration errors without explicitly searching for them. We evaluate DecDNS both formally and empirically. We prove that DecDNS is sound and complete and show that its results agree with widely used DNS software. Finally, we explain how our approach can be integrated into operational practice, helping guide zone management in the real world.
item.dc:creator: Felix Linker, Yue Huang, David Basin, Huayi Duan

item.title: Properties of Public Announcements as Operators: Commutativity, Monotonicity, Idempotence, Fixed Points, and Stabilization
item.description: arXiv:2611.11911v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For each formula $\varphi$, we introduce the public announcement operator $U_\varphi$, which maps every model to its updated model under the public announcement of $\varphi$. We then study its algebraic and dynamic properties with a particular focus on commutativity, monotonicity, idempotence, fixed points, and stabilization. Among many results, we show the following. First, monotonicity of $U_\varphi$ is characterized by a family of preservation conditions and equivalence to an existential formula. Second, there exists a formula that achieves every nonzero ordinal as a stabilization rank---the first stage at which a model stabilizes---of some model. Finally and unexpectedly, extinction of every model under iterated announcements of $\varphi$ is equivalent to common unknowability, being always informative when true, and a fixed point view of the Moore sentence. Over S5, those are further equivalent to common unbelievability and being always informative. Other results include characterizations of commutativity and strong commutativity, idempotence as success, properties of fixed points, and finite and $\omega$-stabilization. For analysis, we use PAL (state elimination) and BPAL (arrow elimination), clarifying their subtle differences.
item.dc:creator: Eiji Yamada

item.title: A Hoare Logic for Continuous-Time Stochastic Processes
item.description: arXiv:2611.12761v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Programming language researchers have developed a wide array of tools to reason about probabilistic programs, but it remains unclear how to apply these proof techniques to continuous-time stochastic processes. To bridge this gap, we propose a verification method for properties of continuous-time stochastic processes by reasoning about them as standard programs. To demonstrate our approach, we define a continuous semantics for a probabilistic imperative language $\mathrm{pWhile}^{\mathrm{dt}}$ by taking the Kuratowski limit of the standard semantics, which collects limit points of the standard program semantics as the time-step approaches zero. Then, we present a Hoare-style logic that uses loop invariants and decreasing functions to verify properties of continuous programs. To establish soundness, we identify a broad class of assertions that are preserved from the standard semantics to the continuous semantics. To demonstrate our approach, we verify properties of ten continuous-time stochastic processes modeled in $\mathrm{pWhile}^{\mathrm{dt}}$, including variants of Brownian motion and a stochastic hybrid system.
item.dc:creator: Kei Imada, Justin Hsu

item.title: zkARc: Succinctly Verifiable Proofs for Neurosymbolic Natural Language Formalization and Verification
item.description: arXiv:2611.10031v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Autonomous agents increasingly execute consequential actions on behalf of users, but ordinary middleware guardrails do not provide cryptographic proof that a policy was actually enforced. Their verdicts leave counterparties dependent on the operator unless they repeat the checks themselves, potentially exposing sensitive policies and inputs. We present zkARc, a modular proof-carrying framework that wraps each stage of Automated Reasoning checks (ARc) in an independent, succinctly verifiable zero-knowledge proof. ARc is a neurosymbolic system that translates natural language policies into formal logic and verifies AI-generated content against them using SMT solvers. zkARc certifies the planner's output, the policy's formalization, the action's formalization and both solver queries. The receipt binds these computations to the exact action received and, under the stated assumptions, reveals no additional information about private policies and intermediate model values beyond the declared public information and verdict. This lets a third party check the claimed policy enforcement without re-running the pipeline or trusting the operator. We prove completeness, knowledge soundness and zero knowledge for the composed receipt under explicit assumptions. An implementation on Qwen2-0.5B enforces a spending policy end to end, approving two purchases and denying a third. A full receipt, which also proves model inference, takes about an hour to issue with CPU-only proving and verifies in under a minute, and the solver proof alone is 88 KiB and verifies in 0.3 seconds.
item.dc:creator: Wyatt Benno (ICME Labs), Alberto Centelles (Imperial College London), Aman Goel (Amazon Web Services), Benjamin Kiesl-Reiter (Amazon Web Services)

item.title: Automata for MSO over Infinite Trees with Quantification over Borel Sets of Branches
item.description: arXiv:2611.10136v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Rabin's Tree Theorem says that the MSO theory of the infinite binary tree $2^*$ is decidable. Shelah showed that MSO logic becomes undecidable if this tree is extended to $2^{\le \omega}$, i.e. by allowing quantification over sets of infinite branches. A longstanding open problem is whether the decidability can be recovered in $2^{\le \omega}$ by restricting set quantification to Borel sets. We make some progress in this direction, by identifying a suitable automaton model, and showing that most of the automata-theoretic approach to Rabin's Theorem can be extended to the new framework. The only missing part is a conjecture about finite-memory determinacy in certain games. This paper states and explores the conjecture. We prove it in some restricted cases, and give lower bounds on the memory required in those games.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: 41st Annual Symposium on Logic in Computer Science (LICS 2026). Leibniz International Proceedings in Informatics (LIPIcs), Volume 380, pp. 21:1-21:24, Schloss Dagstuhl - Leibniz-Zentrum f\"ur Informatik (2026)
item.dc:creator: Miko{\l}aj Boja\'nczyk, Antonio Casares, Sven Manthe, Pawe{\l} Parys

item.title: Extending DBLog-Based Incremental Snapshots to Handle Orphan Rows in CDC Pipelines
item.description: arXiv:2611.10810v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Applications use heterogeneous datastores where a source feeds sinks such as search indexes or data warehouses via change data capture (CDC). As transaction logs have limited retention, CDC alone cannot bootstrap sinks, and traditional approaches either stall source writes or hold back log events. DBLog-based incremental snapshots, adopted by Debezium and Flink CDC, read tables in chunks interleaved with the log without blocking writes or long log stalls and resume where they stopped. After the initial bootstrap, a sink can drift when losing change events or receiving unintended writes. Even a repeated bootstrap can leave orphan rows that exist in the sink and not at the source. A common remedy is to populate a new empty sink, but repairing an existing sink avoids parallel pipelines, a switch and serving traffic from a drifted sink until the new sink is ready. In DBLog's original design, each chunk only emits the latest state of the rows the table still contains, so it does not handle orphan rows. We extend DBLog to delete them using what a chunk read already knows, namely the keys that the range select did not return, emitting a new kind of event that sinks apply as deletes. We also add a repair request that an external process calls with orphan candidates, which the connector checks with its own read, emitting these events for keys confirmed absent. This enables three modes. In the fully integrated mode, every chunk pass removes the orphans it finds during full or periodic repairs. In the second mode, an external drift process hands suspected orphans to the connector. The third mode combines both and is what we recommend. Together, they turn DBLog into a complete data synchronization engine whether a sink catches up on live changes or missing rows, holds wrong column values, or contains orphan rows. Their safety and convergence are formally verified in Isabelle/HOL and Lean 4.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Andreakis

item.title: Factor Rank: A Canonical Algebraic Generalization of Tree Decision Diagrams
item.description: arXiv:2611.10842v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tree decision diagrams (TDDs), recently introduced by Capelli et al. (SAT 2026), are representations of Boolean functions. They generalize OBDDs by replacing variable orders with vtrees. The width of a TDD counts the distinct subfunctions across each vtree cut. Counting subfunctions is blind to linear structure. We introduce algebraic tree decision diagrams (ATDDs) by replacing this count with the rank of the cut matrix. The maximum of these ranks over all cuts, the factor rank, is exactly the width of the ATDD. Every TDD can be converted into an ATDD of no greater width. An ATDD is a tree tensor network in canonical form. ATDDs are exponentially more succinct than TDDs, and quasi-polynomially more succinct than structured deterministic DNNFs. Our main result is that this gain in succinctness does not cost canonicity. ATDDs are the first strict canonical form for a rank-based representation over arbitrary vtrees. For each function and vtree there is exactly one ATDD, over the rationals and without any genericity assumption. The canonicity admits a local characterization. Whether a tree tensor network is the ATDD of the Boolean function it computes can be checked in polynomial time from its tensors alone. Equivalence checking becomes a test of syntactic equality. The operation set includes polynomial-time model counting, weighted model counting, and a test whether a tree tensor network represents a Boolean function. Capelli et al. asked for the complexity of changing the vtree of a TDD and suggested local vtree changes. We answer the question. After a rotation of the vtree at one node, the new ATDD differs from the old one in two tensors only. Vtree change runs in output-polynomial time both for TDDs and for ATDDs. We formalize and verify our core results in Lean. We provide a prototype implementation of TDD and ATDD compilers as a first empirical validation.
item.dc:creator: Alexis de Colnet, Stefan Szeider

item.title: Type-logical grammars and formal languages
item.description: arXiv:2611.12618v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We show that type-logical grammars with the standard rules for product, associativity, extraction and infixation have an NP-complete fixed recognition problem, adapting a construction for first-order linear logic from Pshenitsyn (2025), who already showed that grammars in first-order linear logic are closed under intersection and therefore not semilinear and not mildly context-sensitive. We strengthen these results and shown that grammars in first-order linear logic can simulate the quasi-linear grammars of Book \& Greibach (1970), the grammars recognised in non-deterministic linear time (NSPACE(n) or. NLIN). I argue that NLIN is an interesting class of formal languages as well, and a useful upper bound on the time complexity of formalisms used for natural language, just like LOGCFL is a useful upper bound on the space complexity. Taken together this means that first-order linear logic can be seen as the logic of non-deterministic linear-time string languages, graph languages and automata.
item.dc:creator: Richard Moot (LIRMM,CNRS,LIRMM | PIPL,UM)

item.title: A Logic of Knowledge and Justifications, with an Application to Computational Trust
item.description: arXiv:2405.15647v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a logical framework that enables us to define a formal theory of computational trust in which this notion is analysed in terms of epistemic attitudes towards the possible objects of trust and in relation to existing evidence in favour of the trustworthiness of these objects. The framework is based on a quantified epistemic and justification logic featuring a non-standard handling of identities. Thus, the theory is able to account for the hyperintensional nature of computational trust. We present a proof system and a frame semantics for the logic, we prove soundness and completeness results and we introduce the syntactical machinery required to define a theory of trust.
item.dc:creator: Francesco A. Genco

item.title: Quantifier Elimination and Craig Interpolation, Quantitatively
item.description: arXiv:2501.15156v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantifier elimination (QE) and Craig interpolation (CI) are central to various state-of-the-art automated approaches to hardware- and software verification. They are rooted in the Boolean setting and are successful for, e.g., first-order theories such as linear rational arithmetic. What about their applicability in the quantitative setting where formulae evaluate to numbers and quantitative supremum/infimum quantifiers are the natural counterpart to Boolean quantifiers? Applications include establishing quantitative properties of programs such as bounds on expected outcomes of probabilistic programs featuring non-determinism and analyzing the flow of information through programs. In this paper, we present, to the best of our knowledge, the first QE algorithm for possibly unbounded, $\infty$- or $(-\infty)$-valued, or discontinuous piecewise linear quantities. They are the quantitative counterpart to linear rational arithmetic, and they are a popular quantitative assertion language for probabilistic program verification. We provide rigorous soundness proofs as well as upper bounds on the size of the output. Moreover, we present two applications of our QE algorithm. First, our algorithm yields a quantitative CI theorem: Given arbitrary piecewise linear quantities $f,g$ with $f \models g$ (i.e., $f$ is at most $g$ at every variable valuation), both the strongest and the weakest Craig interpolants are quantifier-free and effectively constructible. Such interpolants lie between the two quantities and use only their common free variables. Second, we apply our QE algorithm to computing minimal and maximal expected outcomes of loop-free probabilistic programs featuring unbounded non-determinism, and to checking inductivity of candidate upper bounds on minimal and maximal expected outcomes of probabilistic loops featuring unbounded non-determinism.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Batz, Joost-Pieter Katoen, Nora Orhan

item.title: Constructing Witnesses for Lower Bounds on Behavioural Distances
item.description: arXiv:2504.08639v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Behavioural distances provide a robust alternative to notions of equivalence such as bisimilarity in the context of probabilistic transition systems. They can be defined as least fixed points, whose universal property allows us to exhibit upper bounds on the distance between states, showing them to be at most some distance apart. In this paper, we instead consider the problem of bounding distances from below, showing states to be at least some distance apart. Contrary to upper bounds, it is possible to reason about lower bounds inductively. We exploit this by giving an inductive derivation system for lower bounds on an existing definition of behavioural distance for labelled Markov chains. This is inspired by recent work on apartness as an inductive counterpart to bisimilarity. Proofs in our system will be shown to closely match the behavioural distance by soundness and (approximate) completeness results. We further provide a constructive correspondence between our derivation system and formulas in a modal logic with quantitative semantics. This logic was used in recent work of Rady and van Breugel to construct evidence for lower bounds on behavioural distances. Our constructions provide smaller witnessing formulas in many examples.
item.dc:creator: Ruben Turkenburg, Harsh Beohar, Franck van Breugel, Clemens Kupke, Jurriaan Rot

item.title: Inquisitive Team Semantics of LTL
item.description: arXiv:2505.10700v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In recent years, hyperproperties (i.e., properties of sets of traces) have been identified as a crucial concept for capturing information-flow security policies and knowledge of agents in distributed systems. In the synchronous linear-time setting, a well-known approach for the specification of hyperproperties is based on the set semantics of standard LTL. The resulting logic (TeamLTL) inherits the powerful split interpretation of disjunction from dependence logic. In this paper, we introduce a novel team semantics of LTL inspired by inquisitive logic, whose main features are the intuitionistic interpretation of implication and the inquisitive semantics of disjunction. We investigate expressiveness, decidability, and complexity issues of the novel logic that we call InqLTL and its extension with strong negation. We show that InqLTL with strong negation is highly undecidable and strictly less expressive than TeamLTL with strong negation. On the positive side, we identify a meaningful fragment of InqLTL with a decidable model-checking problem that can express relevant classes of hyperproperties. To the best of our knowledge, this fragment represents the first hyper logic with a decidable model-checking problem that allows unrestricted use of temporal modalities and conditional second-order universal quantification over system refinements via intuitionistic implication.
item.dc:creator: Laura Bozzelli, Tadeusz Litak, Munyque Mittelmann, Aniello Murano

item.title: Recursive Program Synthesis from Sketches and Mixed-Quantifier Properties
item.description: arXiv:2601.04045v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a novel approach for the synthesis of recursive programs from relational, mixed-quantifier first-order logic properties. We solve this problem using a sketching-based, enumerative, counterexample-guided approach. Our algorithm learns syntactic constraints from counterexamples to prune the candidate space and employs a prophylactic pruning technique to avoid enumerating invalid candidates altogether. We implement our technique in a tool called Cataclyst and evaluate it on a suite of 60 benchmarks. We demonstrate that both counterexample generalization and prophylactic pruning significantly improve performance. Cataclyst solves 59/60 benchmarks, while variants of Cataclyst without counterexample generalization or prophylactic pruning solve fewer benchmarks. No existing tool can directly handle the entire class of synthesis problems that our tool can. A portfolio of existing state-of-the-art tools solves 30/60 of our benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Derek Egolf, Stavros Tripakis

item.title: Almost Symmetric Linear Arc Monadic Datalog and Transitive Tournaments
item.description: arXiv:2606.24711v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce $n$-almost symmetric Datalog and study $n$-almost symmetric linear arc monadic Datalog. We characterize the finite relational structures whose constraint satisfaction problem is solved by this Datalog fragment as those that can be primitive positively constructed from the transitive tournament on $n+2$ vertices. We also give characterizations in terms of a certain homomorphism duality (which we call $n$-fixed unfolded caterpillar duality) and in universal-algebraic terms (the existence of $k$-absorptive operations and of operations forming an elevator chain of length $n+1$). This article generalizes the results from Bodirsky and Starke about symmetric linear arc monadic Datalog.
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Meyer, Florian Starke

item.title: Exponential Lower Bounds for Horn Amalgamation
item.description: arXiv:2608.12206v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The amalgamation decision problem asks whether the finite models of a given universal first-order sentence have the amalgamation property. We prove that this problem is ExpTime-hard for universal Horn sentences of maximum relation arity three, and 2ExpTime-hard when the arity is unbounded, thereby strengthening the previous best lower bounds for universal Horn sentences. The first reduction simulates runs of nondeterministic tree automata using a single ternary relation and unary and binary auxiliary relations. The second simulates finite winning strategies in an exponential corridor game. As a secondary contribution, we prove that deciding the winner remains 2ExpTime-complete for the game normal form used in our reduction, in which each move label determines a unique legal successor from every non-winning legal row.
item.dc:creator: Jakub Rydval

item.title: A Non-Dichotomy for CSPs of Stable $\omega$-Categorical Structures
item.description: arXiv:2610.19940v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We construct countable, stable, $\omega$-categorical structures with at most two binary relations whose CSPs exhibit three complexity regimes: NP-complete, decidable but not in NP, and undecidable. The templates arise from a controlled Hrushovski construction of stable $\omega$-categorical graphs $M_\alpha$ for suitable irrational parameters $\alpha>1$. Some of these graphs have NP-complete CSPs. Expanding the graphs $M_\alpha$ by the non-edge relation turns age membership into a restriction of the CSP. For every time-constructible bound $t$, there is such an expansion whose CSP is decidable but not in DTIME$(t)$. For an explicit parameter $\alpha$, the restriction to complete instances belongs to $\mathrm{coNP}$ and the full CSP belongs to $\Sigma_2^{\mathrm P}$. Separating the ages of the $M_\alpha$ using graphs with large girth and prescribed density yields $2^{\aleph_0}$ distinct CSPs of these expansions, all but countably many of which are undecidable.
item.dc:creator: Manuel Bodirsky, David Bradley-Williams, Ehud Hrushovski, Christoph Spiess

item.title: DAPS: Dependency-Aware Premise Selection for LLM Theorem Proving
item.description: arXiv:2610.41536v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM-based theorem proving in Lean 4 has advanced rapidly, but provers are difficult to leverage newly contributed lemmas, because retrieval skews toward popular foundational lemmas, leaving the right premises buried among hundreds of thousands of candidates. Existing neural selectors rank candidates by semantic similarity, with three intrinsic limitations: frequency-skewed retrieval, isolated pairwise ranking, and degradation on out-of-distribution queries such as competition problems and informal language. Given that mathematics is structured by dependencies rather than similarities, we restore this signal to both the training data and the model. We curate two underused dependency resources. We conduct the first systematic mining of 53 Lean Blueprint projects, a previously untapped corpus of 3,805 manually curated informal+formal nodes that capture rare, research-level premises absent from Mathlib4. We further pair it with the extraction of comprehensive, typed, multi-level Mathlib4 dependencies. We then introduce DAPS, a dependency-aware premise selector with a structural neighborhood encoder, a group-level contrastive objective, and a Mathlib-then-Blueprint adaptation procedure. DAPS reaches 78.74 Recall@16 on Mathlib4-Heldout (+11.41 over the strong selector LeanHammer) and widens the margin to 7xrecall on competition-style queries. Downstream, its selected premises raise Goedel-Prover-V2-8B Pass@4 on miniF2F-test from 49.90 to 54.03 and improve all four general-purpose LLMs on the informal IMO-ProofBench (up to +11.4% relative). Project page: https://daps-eth.github.io/.
item.dc:creator: Zixuan Chen, Wenyuan Jiang, Junling Wang, Mrinmaya Sachan, Yinya Huang

item.title: Learning temporal formulas from examples is hard
item.description: arXiv:2312.16336v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the problem of learning linear temporal logic (LTL) formulas from examples, as a first step towards expressing a property separating positive and negative instances in a way that is comprehensible for humans. Given positive and negative words, the goal is to find a smallest formula satisfied by the positive words and not by the negative ones. We study the computational complexity of this problem for all fragments of negation-free LTL built from the operators F (eventually), G (globally), X (next), $\wedge$ (conjunction), and $\vee$ (disjunction), without the until operator. We show that the problem is in NP for all fragments, that it is in polynomial time for the fragments containing none of the pairs $\{X,\wedge\}$, $\{X,\vee\}$, $\{F,\wedge\}$ and $\{G,\vee\}$, and that it is NP-complete for all other fragments, already for alphabets with two or three letters. We also show that the fragment with only X and $\wedge$ has a polynomial time 3-approximation algorithm, but no polynomial time approximation scheme unless P = NP. These results motivate the search for efficient heuristics.
item.dc:creator: Corto Mascle, Nathana\"el Fijalkow, Guillaume Lagarde

item.title: Graded String Diagrams with Applications in Probabilistic Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2501.18404v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce string diagrams for graded symmetric monoidal categories. Our approach includes a definition of graded monoidal theory and the corresponding freely generated syntactic category. The para construction on monoidal actegories is a motivating example for our framework, and we show how an axiomatic presentation of the resulting category $\mathbf{Para}(\mathbb{G},\mathbf{C})$ may be modularly obtained from presentations for $\mathbb{G}$ and $\mathbf{C}$. We demonstrate three different applications of our diagrammatic language under the same theme: probabilistic reasoning. First, we show how to axiomatise a variant of the graded category $\mathbf{ImP}$, recently introduced by Liell-Cock and Staton to model imprecise probability. This culminates in a representation, as string diagrams with grading wires, of programs with primitives for nondeterministic and probabilistic choices and conditioning. Second, we exploit our modular presentation result to provide a new proof for a presentation of $\mathbf{Gauss}$, the category of Gaussian stochastic maps. Third, we use grading wires to represent causal interventions on Bayesian networks.
item.dc:creator: Ralph Sarkis, Fabio Zanasi

item.title: For Generalised Algebraic Theories, Two Sorts Are Enough
item.description: arXiv:2601.19426v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generalised algebraic theories (GATs) allow multiple sorts indexed over each other. For example, the theories of categories or Martin-L{\"o}f type theories form GATs. Categories have two sorts, objects and morphisms, and the latter are double-indexed over the former. Martin-L{\"o}f type theory has four sorts: contexts, substitutions, types and terms. For example, types are indexed over contexts, and terms are indexed over both contexts and types. In this paper we show that any GAT can be reduced to a GAT with only two sorts, and there is a section-retraction correspondence (formally, a strict coreflection) between models of the original and the reduced GAT. In particular, any model of the original GAT can be turned into a model of the reduced (two-sorted) GAT and back, and this roundtrip is the identity. The reduced GAT is simpler than the original GAT in the following aspects: it does not have sort equalities; it does not have interleaved sorts and operations; if the original GAT did not have interleaved sorts and operations, then the reduced GAT won't have operations interleaved between different sorts. In a type-theoretic metatheory, the initial algebra of a GAT is called a quotient inductive-inductive type (QIIT). Our reduction provides a way to implement QIITs with sort equalities or interleaved constructors which are not allowed by Cubical Agda. An instance of our reduction is the well-known method of reducing mutual inductive types to a single indexed family. Our approach is semantic in that it does not rely on a syntactic description of GATs, but instead, on Uemura's bi-initial characterisation of the category of (finite) GATs in the 2-category of finitely complete categories with a chosen exponentiable morphism.
item.dc:creator: Samy Avrillon, Ambrus Kaposi, Ambroise Lafont, Niyousha Najmaei, Johann Rosain

item.title: Viverra: Text-to-Code with Guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2605.14972v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A fundamental limitation of Text-to-Code is that no guarantee can be obtained about the correctness of the generated code. Therefore, to ensure its correctness, the generated code still has to be reviewed, tested, and maintained by developers. However, parsing through LLM-generated code can be tedious and time-consuming, potentially negating the productivity gains promised by AI-coding tools. To address this challenge, we present Viverra, a system that automatically produces formally verified annotations alongside generated code to aid user's understanding of the generated program. Given a natural-language task description, Viverra prompts an LLM to synthesize a C program together with candidate assertions expressing safety and correctness properties. It then verifies those assertions in a compositional and best-effort manner via a portfolio of bounded model checkers. Evaluation on 17 diverse programming tasks suggests that Viverra can efficiently generate code with verified assertions, and that these assertions improve users' performance on code-comprehension tasks in a user study with more than 400 task completions.
item.dc:creator: Haoze Wu, Rocky Klopfenstein, Keith Farkas, Nina Narodytska

item.title: Learning How to Cube
item.description: arXiv:2605.16632v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Despite the effectiveness of Cube-and-Conquer (C&C) for solving challenging Boolean Satisfiability (SAT) problems, no prior work has shown that transformer-based models can learn effective cubing heuristics. We introduce a neuro-symbolic post-training framework for this task. We design an MCTS-based data curation pipeline that uses symbolic heuristics to explore splitting decisions over SAT competition formulas, producing preference data grounded in solver statistics and augmented with reasoning traces from a teacher model. Our two-stage post-training, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by direct preference optimization (DPO), enables a 4B-parameter model to achieve a pass@5 score of 53 on 100 SAT competition benchmarks, surpassing frontier LLMs such as Claude-Sonnet-4 (50) and matching, with five attempts per benchmark, the best symbolic heuristic (53), which nonetheless remains preferable for a single attempt. Ablations show that SFT alone improves pass@5 from 46 to 51, with DPO adding 2 additional benchmarks; an entropy/agreement ablation on realized first-cube decisions further shows that SFT, not DPO, accounts for the root-level decision diversity that produces complementary per-run coverage over deterministic symbolic methods. This demonstrates that transformers can be trained to make effective cubing decisions in a domain traditionally dominated by symbolic methods.
item.dc:creator: Ferhat Erata, Sam Kouteili, Thanos Typaldos, Timos Antonopoulos, Robert B. Jones, Byron Cook, Ruzica Piskac

item.title: Alternating Abduction and Planning over Temporal Dynamic Knowledge Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2607.27287v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Knowledge graphs change over time, but the effects of actions on them are only partly stated: the ontology entails further consequences, facts that an action needs are often unknown, and an action may make the graph inconsistent. We study these problems for Temporal Dynamic Knowledge Graphs (TDKGs), that is, SROIQ knowledge bases whose actions are rules with delete/insert templates and whose events lie on an intrinsic timeline. We present three tools that use a SROIQ reasoner only through a few operations: temporal projection, which plays the events along the timeline and is the exact test of plans; DDA (Direct-Derivation Abduction), which explains an observation by assuming its negation and negating what the reasoner newly derives; and APT (Abduction and Planning over TDKGs), which plans backwards from a goal, assumes the facts that the plan needs but nobody stated, and lets DDA explain the assumptions, each explanation becoming a new goal for a sub-plan, up to a depth bound. The same machinery synthesises action sequences that end in a chosen contradiction. We prove that projection is decidable and that the indirect effects of an action are exactly the entailments of the updated state; that DDA is sound, terminates and finds every single-assertion explanation; and that APT is sound and terminates, while bounded planning is decidable but 2NExpTime-hard. We compare the tools analytically with hitting-set abduction and classical planning, compare DDA with the abduction solver CATS on shared problems, and run them on six benchmarks. Five reasoners (HermiT, Konclude, Pellet, Openllet, JFact) return identical results. Their incremental modes answered some checks wrongly after removals and gave no speed-up; parallel calls help only when a single call is expensive.
item.dc:creator: Amir Hossein Sharafi, Alireza Shahbazi

item.title: Certified but Private: Scalable Zero-Knowledge Proofs for Neural Network Guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2608.17070v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: With the growing deployment of machine learning models, formal guarantees of the robustness and fairness of these models have become increasingly important in safety-critical and legal-compliance settings. However, model parameters are often commercial secrets that cannot be disclosed to auditors or end users. To this end, we present PANDA, a scalable system that uses zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) to prove the robustness and fairness properties of a model without revealing its private parameters. PANDA is built on top of CROWN, an efficient robustness certification framework that is used in many state-of-the-art formal verification tools for neural networks. The core contribution of PANDA is a novel algorithm for proving linear relaxation bounds for non-linear activation layers, yielding simple, lightweight proofs. Remarkably, our implementation can generate proofs of local robustness for neural networks with more than 2.9M parameters in 5 minutes, and can verify them in 10 seconds. Prior ZKP-based robustness system rely on exponential-time algorithms that cannot scale to nontrivial networks. In contrast, PANDA scales polynomially in the number of neurons in a network, allowing us to support neural networks 4 orders of magnitude larger than previous approaches with significantly reduced prover overhead.
item.dc:creator: Youwei Zhong, Ben Merbaum, Timos Antonopoulos, Ning Luo, Charalampos Papamanthou, Katerina Sotiraki, Ruzica Piskac

item.title: Symbolic Temporal Supervision of LLM Agents Using Contracts
item.description: arXiv:2609.18128v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents augmented by tools can automate complex, multi-step tasks, such as web navigation, code generation, and workflow orchestration, by acting on external systems through tool calls. However, hallucinations, distributional instability, and adversarial manipulations in LLMs, and the irreversible consequences of certain tool calls can lead to harmful outcomes. These risks call for safeguards that can check requirements across a trajectory, both before actions execute and when recorded behavior is evaluated. We present ContrAgent, a contract-based framework for symbolic temporal supervision of LLM agents. ContrAgent captures an agent's behavior as a sequence of tool calls and formalizes it as a trace over a fixed set of checkable predicates. It then specifies required behaviors using assume-guarantee contracts in linear temporal logic over finite traces (LTL$_f$). Each contract is compiled to a deterministic finite automaton (DFA) that serves two roles: gating agent actions online and evaluating recorded traces offline. A contract library, acting as a reusable knowledge base, is maintained independently of the agent's model and can be applied across different agents within the same task domain. We show the effectiveness of our approach on four benchmarks spanning both roles, where ContrAgent is competitive with LLM-judge, classifier, and guardrail baselines while producing deterministic, reproducible verdicts and, in the online mode, orders of magnitude lower per-call latency.
item.dc:creator: Yifeng Xiao, Johnna Liu, Pierluigi Nuzzo

item.title: A Calculus for Units of Measure with Conversion
item.description: arXiv:2609.38242v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Programs that compute with physical quantities often need to convert between units of measurement, and as the Mars Climate Orbiter showed, these conversions can be a rich source of errors. Meanwhile, typed unit calculi, our most rigorous formalisms for checking physical units in a program, have excluded unit conversions. Through this exclusion, they have established a powerful property: well-typed programs are invariant under rescaling (no program can depend on how big a meter is). But losing the ability to convert between units is a significant cost. In contrast, practical languages provide conversion but no invariance theorem. We present $\Lambda_S$, a typed lambda calculus with conversion, quantification over units and dimensions, and vectors and linear maps with per-component units, and we determine exactly how much invariance survives conversion. For terms without unit constants we prove two abstraction theorems: (i) a convert-free term is invariant under every rescaling; (ii) a term with conversions is invariant under every rescaling that scales all units of one dimension by the same factor. The condition in (ii) cannot be weakened: under any other rescaling, some conversion of a nonzero value is not invariant. For first-order programs, a verified decision procedure returns one of three verdicts: it certifies that no error in the declared conversion factors can change the program's answer, names the accumulated ratio through which such an error would scale it, or declines. A verified checker decides whether unit declarations are consistent and determine every conversion factor, and extracts each factor exactly. We also prove adequacy, erasure, and the $n$-variable Pi theorem of dimensional analysis with conversion. Every theorem is mechanized in Lean 4, and the evaluator compiles to a native binary.
item.dc:creator: Eric Allen

item.title: Quantitative Verification of Infinite-State Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.11991v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Many network protocols and distributed systems combine recursion, unbounded local state, and quantitative behaviour such as cost, latency, or reliability. Existing decidability results for networks of pushdown systems are largely qualitative, and do not extend to quantitative analyses, which must jointly track traces and weights. We present a framework for the quantitative verification of acyclic networks of weighted pushdown systems. Finitely summarising a recursive network component requires collapsing the infinite family of runs obtained by pumping its nested loops, and doing so exactly, rather than by over-approximation, is a standing difficulty. We give a class of weight domains where this is possible: pumping semirings, those in which the weights accumulated by such a family collapse to a closed form; informally, the domain must be unable to count iterations. The class admits domains with infinite ascending chains, such as the arctic semiring and downward-closed languages. Over these, we give a terminating saturation algorithm computing quantitative reachability exactly, resting on two ideas: segment tree algebras, a compositional representation of runs, and thermal extensions, which symbolically separate accelerated weights so that further acceleration remains exact. We use this to compute upward and downward closures of context-free languages uniformly, and to lift the algorithm to acyclic networks over "thin" pumping semirings, yielding the first quantitative safety and reachability analyses for networks of pushdown systems.
item.dc:creator: Dhruv Nevatia, David Basin

item.title: The Logic of Emergence
item.description: arXiv:2611.06641v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: ``Emergence'' refers to the fact that different mathematical languages and theories seem to be required to describe scientific theories that operate at different spatial and temporal scales. Highly circumscribed, special cases of emergence have been investigated using many different formal tools, including coarse-graining (over space and / or time), renormalization, dimension reduction, broken symmetry, and various formulations of causality. Here we extend the mathematics of model theory to unify and extend these earlier investigations. As a preliminary application of our framework, we investigate canonical examples of emergence, including the emergence of genetics from chemistry, of psychology from neurobiology, and of different forms of collective behavior from the laws governing their constituent parts. By exploiting the power of model theory we also uncover many aspects of emergence that were previously obscured. In particular, we uncover some of the rich hierarchical structure that relates different scientific fields. For example, we show that scientific fields can be related via a collection of multiple partial orders, all defined over the same set. On the other hand, under an alternative relation among scientific fields, one which allows cycles, we show that it is possible that the set of all of scientific fields must collapse into a single scientific field. Going forward, these investigations point to the formal tools that might need to be developed in order to arrive at a deeper understanding of this emergent hierarchy of scientific reality.
item.dc:creator: David H. Wolpert, David C. Krakauer
